title: Reduce reactions to accidental peanut exposure through oral immunotherapy

concept.text: Raise the reaction threshold in peanut-allergic patients through standardized oral desensitisation. This reduces risk during ongoing treatment but does not establish permanent, treatment-free tolerance. Proposed completion test: FDA approval for mitigation of reactions after accidental exposure, supported by a randomized phase 3 food-challenge trial demonstrating an increased proportion tolerating a 600 mg peanut-protein challenge after approximately one year of treatment. Test set by: FDA; the PALISADE/ARC003 programme used controlled oral challenge as a surrogate for mitigation of accidental-exposure reactions. Reported achieved: FDA approved Palforzia on 31 January 2020. Overlaps: CLM-01, IMM-04, PHA-04, DER-07. Sources given: [FDA Palforzia approval record](https://www.fda.gov/vaccines-blood-biologics/allergenics/palforzia) ; [FDA Palforzia regulatory assessment](https://www.fda.gov/media/135328/download).

page.title: Peanut oral immunotherapy for desensitisation
page.definition: Children with peanut allergy receive increasing doses of peanut protein followed by daily maintenance, raising the amount they can ingest without dose-limiting allergic symptoms. This on-treatment effect is called desensitisation; it does not establish tolerance after treatment stops.

goal.need: In 2020, an estimated one million US children had peanut allergy, and only about one in five was expected to outgrow it. Even careful avoidance can fail. Raising the amount of peanut a child can eat before symptoms develop gives some protection when a food contains peanut unexpectedly. That protection depends on continued dosing. Children still avoid peanut and carry epinephrine, because accidental exposures and treatment doses can both cause anaphylaxis.

completion.title: A regulator authorises peanut oral immunotherapy for desensitisation in children with peanut allergy.
completion.criterion: A medicines regulator authorises at least one oral peanut-allergen product for children with confirmed peanut allergy to mitigate reactions to accidental peanut exposure. Evidence of desensitisation shows that, during treatment, children can ingest a greater amount of peanut protein without dose-limiting symptoms than controls can. A double-blind, placebo-controlled oral food challenge measures that amount in milligrams of peanut protein at a protocol-defined dose.
completion.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration paediatric indication and European Union marketing authorisation for peanut desensitisation. The European Medicines Agency’s clinical-development guideline specifies the food-challenge measure.
completion.threshold_quote: Palforzia was granted marketing authorisation in the EU on 17 December 2020 for desensitisation of children and adolescents to peanut allergy.
completion.basis: FDA first licensed Palforzia on 31 January 2020 for treatment starting at ages 4–17. In PALISADE, 250 of 372 treated participants and 5 of 124 placebo participants in that age group tolerated a single dose of at least 600 mg with no more than mild symptoms after approximately 24 weeks of maintenance. The difference was 63.2 percentage points (95% CI 53.0–73.3). The EU authorised Palforzia in December 2020. In July 2024 the US indication expanded to allow initiation at ages 1–3 as well. The evidence establishes desensitisation during dosing with continued peanut avoidance. FDA required a risk-management programme because dosing can cause anaphylaxis.

milestones.title: Peanut-allergic children tolerate 3.9 g cumulative peanut protein after oral immunotherapy.
milestones.criterion: After maintenance at 300 mg peanut protein daily, assess whether children complete an open oral challenge of 300, 600, 1,200 and 1,800 mg peanut protein at 30-minute intervals. Stop at objective symptoms or 3.9 g cumulative. The protocol tested the first cohort after 13–22 months of maintenance and the second after 4–7 months.
milestones.set_by: Duke University Medical Center and Arkansas Children's Hospital investigators, Jones et al.'s published peanut oral immunotherapy protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: The OFC was discontinued at 3.9 g or with objective symptoms.

milestones.title: More AR101 recipients than controls tolerate 300 mg of peanut protein in one dose, 443 mg cumulative.
milestones.criterion: In ARC001, enrol participants aged 4–26 with dose-limiting symptoms at or below 143 mg cumulative peanut protein on screening challenge. Compare responder proportions by randomised group at the 0.05 significance level. A responder tolerates a 300 mg challenge dose (443 mg cumulative) with no more than mild symptoms at the exit double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge after two weeks at the 300 mg/day maintenance level or matched placebo.
milestones.set_by: Allergen Research Corporation, ARC001 protocol amendment 3, primary clinical efficacy endpoint, NCT01987817.
milestones.threshold_quote: tolerate at least 300 mg (443 mg cumulative) of peanut protein with no more than mild symptoms at the exit DBPCFC

milestones.title: The lower 95% confidence bound for AR101’s 600 mg responder advantage exceeds 15 percentage points.
milestones.criterion: For PALISADE’s North American endpoint, compare responder proportions in the intention-to-treat population aged 4–17. A responder tolerates a single dose of at least 600 mg peanut protein (1,043 mg cumulative through that dose) with no more than mild symptoms at the exit double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge after approximately 24 weeks at 300 mg/day or matched placebo. Count withdrawals and missing exit challenges as nonresponses. The lower bound of the Farrington–Manning 95% confidence interval for AR101 minus placebo must exceed 15 percentage points.
milestones.set_by: Aimmune Therapeutics, PALISADE protocol amendment 4.0, section 9.2.1, North American primary endpoint, NCT02635776.
milestones.threshold_quote: lower bound of the corresponding test-based 95% confidence interval is greater than the pre-specified margin of 0.15.

milestones.title: A child tolerates a previously reactive amount of peanut during oral immunotherapy.
milestones.criterion: In a child with clinical peanut allergy, document the amount ingested and the symptoms at the initial exposure assessment. During oral immunotherapy, document ingestion of that amount or more without the symptoms that limited the initial dose.
milestones.set_by: European Academy of Allergy and Clinical Immunology, clinical definition of desensitisation applied to an individual patient.
milestones.threshold_quote: the ability to consume a defined amount of the food without dose-limiting symptoms

milestones.title: Children receiving oral peanut flour tolerate more peanut protein at blinded challenge than controls.
milestones.criterion: Randomly assign children with peanut allergy to oral peanut flour or placebo. Compare the cumulative amount of peanut protein the groups can ingest at a double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge during treatment. The treated group must tolerate more. In the Varshney protocol, the challenge took place at about one year, after four weeks of maintenance, and stopped at a maximum of 5,000 mg cumulative.
milestones.set_by: European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, food-allergy efficacy measure, as implemented in the Varshney trial.
milestones.threshold_quote: the tolerated food dose in a double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge

results.finding: After oral immunotherapy, 27 of 29 peanut-allergic children completed the 3.9 g cumulative peanut protein challenge.
results.detail: Ten of 39 enrolled children withdrew before challenge. Two challenged children stopped after 2.1 g, one because of parental anxiety and the other because of mild urticaria and one episode of vomiting.
results.quote: Of 29 subjects who completed the protocol, 27 ingested 3.9 g peanut protein during food challenge.

results.finding: In children with peanut allergy (28 randomized, 25 challenged), oral peanut flour increased the median tolerated cumulative dose by 4,720 mg versus placebo.
results.detail: Three children assigned to peanut flour withdrew before the challenge because of allergic side effects. The median difference is calculated from the reported challenge doses, with the treated median at the protocol ceiling.
results.quote: During the double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge, all remaining peanut OIT subjects (N=16) ingested the maximum cumulative dose of 5000 mg (approximately 20 peanuts), while placebo subjects (N=9) ingested a median cumulative dose of 280 mg (range, 0-1900 mg) [p<0.001].

results.finding: Among 146 children with peanut allergy, the median cumulative dose tolerated at the blinded challenge was 5,000 mg higher with oral peanut flour than with placebo.
results.detail: The methods specify a 5,000 mg cumulative challenge maximum. The results report a median cumulative tolerated dose of 5,005 mg in the peanut flour group.

results.finding: In 496 children with peanut allergy, PALFORZIA increased the rate of tolerating 600 mg peanut protein with no more than mild symptoms by 63.2 percentage points versus placebo.
results.detail: Study 1 counted children who missed the exit challenge as nonresponders. The 95% CI for the treatment difference was 53.0 to 73.3 percentage points.

results.finding: In ARC003 (496 children with peanut allergy), Palforzia increased the responder rate by 63.2 percentage points versus placebo at the primary challenge dose.
results.detail: The 95% confidence interval for the response-rate difference was 53.0 to 73.3 percentage points.
